questions.text: When an episode visits the same state twice, how do first-visit and every-visit Monte Carlo evaluation differ?

options.A: First-visit uses only the first visit’s return; every-visit uses returns from both visits.
options.B: First-visit uses only immediate rewards; every-visit uses discounted returns.
options.C: First-visit uses the model’s transitions; every-visit uses sampled episodes.
options.D: First-visit updates after each step; every-visit waits until the episode ends.

questions.explanation: First-visit counts a state once per episode at its first occurrence; every-visit counts every occurrence and its following return.

questions.text: A policy changes during Monte Carlo control, but its state-value estimate is an average over every return since training began. Which update choice helps the estimate track the newer policy more quickly?

options.A: Use a constant step size α so recent returns retain substantial weight.
options.B: Keep the 1/n step size so older returns dominate as n grows.
options.C: Stop sampling new episodes after each policy improvement.
options.D: Replace every observed return with a fixed terminal reward.

questions.explanation: A constant step size keeps reacting to new returns, whereas the sample-average step size 1/n becomes very small as the count grows.

questions.text: A first-visit evaluator sees trajectory states [s, t, s] with returns [5, 3, 1]. Its seen set starts empty and it skips a state already seen in this episode. Which return updates V(s)?

options.A: Only 1, because the last visit is closest to episode end.
options.B: Both 5 and 1, because both visits appear in the trajectory.
options.C: The average 3, because the two visits are merged before update.
options.D: Only 5, because the later visit is skipped after s is marked seen.

questions.explanation: The first s is processed with return 5 and added to seen. When s appears again, the code continues without updating it.
